sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Rāvaṇa** ​(*ravana*) — ‌Ten-Headed King, ‌Lanka · ​The ​ruler of ​Laṅkā and ​chief of ​the ‌Rākṣasas, whose ​destruction by ​Rāmacandra forms ‌the subject ​of ‌the Rāmāyaṇa ​— belongs ‌to the ​Sanskrit ​tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under ​the ‌domain "Ten-Headed ​King, Lanka". ‌The name ​means ‌"The ruler ​of Laṅkā ‌and chief ​of ‌the Rākṣasas, ​whose destruction ​by Rāmacandra ‌forms the ‌subject ‌of the ​Rāmāyaṇa"[^1].

**Rāvaṇa** ​belongs to ‌the ​Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ‌is associated ​with ​ten-headed king, ‌lanka.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ​as **Rāvaṇa** ​and serves ​its temple ​at ‌[ravana.com](https://punicodex.com/ravana/). The ‌restoration preserves ​at least ‌one ​distinctive feature ​— a ‌diacritic or ‌a distinctive ‌letter ‌— that ​the ASCII ‌form loses, ​and ​exactly one ​historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, ​which places ​the name ‌in Tier ​1. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*ravana* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Devanagari ‌as **रावण**. ​Etymologically it ​means "The ​ruler of ​Laṅkā and ​chief of ‌the Rākṣasas, ​whose destruction ​by Rāmacandra ‌forms the ​subject of ‌the Rāmāyaṇa"[^1].

​Sanskrit Rāvaṇa, ‌from the ​causative of ​rū 'to ​roar, to ​cry'; the ​ten-headed king ‌of Lanka.

​The ASCII ‌form *ravana* ​survives only ‌because the ​early domain-name ‌system could ​not carry ‌diacritics; it ​is a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ‌ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Rāvaṇa** ​recovers the ‌vowel length ​of the ​original directly ‌in the ​address bar. ​The restoration ‌preserves at least ​one distinctive ‌feature — ​a diacritic ​or a ​distinctive letter ​— that ‌the ASCII ‌form loses, ​and exactly ‌one historically ​valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ‌which places ‌the name ‌in Tier ‌1.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**r** → ​**R** — ​Same, capitalized
‌- **a** ​→ **ā** ​— Macron: ​long vowel
‌- **v** ​→ **v** ​— Same
​- **a** ‌→ **a** ​— Same
‌- **n** ​→ **ṇ** ‌— N ​with dot: ‌retroflex n
‌- **a** ​→ **a** ​— Same

​The canonical ​temple for ‌this name ‌is served ​at **ravana.com**[^2].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the ​name is ​**/ravana/** ​— ​Sanskrit ‌Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

​- ‌**R** ​— Initial ‌character ​of ​the ​restored ​form ​Rāvaṇa.
‌- ​**āvaṇa** ‌— Remainder ​of ‌the ​name, ‌preserving ​the ‌distinctive ​marks ​of ‌the ‌Sanskrit tradition.

‌For ​the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: ​'RAVANA' ‌— pronounce ​the ‌restored ​form ​with ​attention ​to ‌the ‌preserved ​diacritics ‌and length.

​Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms ‌of ‌the ​name:

‌- ​**Sanskrit** ​— Rāvaṇa, ​the ‌restored ​Unicode ​form ​of ‌the ​name

​Rāvaṇa ​is Tier ‌1 ​because ‌the ​Sanskrit ‌form ​preserves ‌distinctive ‌features ​that ​ASCII loses: ​stress, ​length, ‌or ‌special ​characters.

sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌**Rāvaṇa** circulate ‌within ​the Sanskrit ​corpus, where ​the ​figure embodies ​ten-headed king, ‌lanka.[^1]

​### Primary ​Attestation (Sources)

‌Rāvaṇa ​is attested ‌in the ​canonical ‌Sanskrit sources ​as a ​figure ​associated with ​ten-headed king, ​lanka.[^2]

‌### Name ​and ‌Meaning (Etymology)

​The name ‌means ​"The ruler ‌of Laṅkā ​and ‌chief of ​the Rākṣasas, ​whose ‌destruction by ‌Rāmacandra forms ‌the ​subject of ​the Rāmāyaṇa" ‌and ​reflects the ​figure's role ‌in ​the tradition. ​**Rāvaṇa** is ‌the ​ten-headed king ‌of Laṅkā ​and ​the antagonist ​of the ​*Rāmāyaṇa*. ‌A devout ‌śaiva and ​master ‌of the ​Vedas, he ​abducts ‌Sītā and ‌is ultimately ‌defeated ‌by Rāma, ​the avatāra ‌of ​Viṣṇu.[^1] His ​character is ​morally ‌complex: the ​epic ​praises his ​learning and ‌power ​even as ​it condemns ​his ‌lust and ​tyranny. His ‌ten ​heads traditionally ‌represent mastery ​of ‌the four ‌Vedas and ​six ​shastras, making ​him a ​scholar-king ‌as well ‌as a ​demon.[^2]
